newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian investors in new march, plan Tirana rally.
newsitem.headline: Albanian investors in new march, plan Tirana rally.

text.p: Tens of thousands of Albanians ruined by failed investment schemes surged through this port for the third consecutive day on Friday to denounce the Balkan country's right-wing government.
The resumption of last month's protests, which triggered mass arrests, spread to the capital Tirana, where up to 1,000 demonstrators demanded the return of lost savings but were dispersed by police.

Opposition parties, hoping to inspire disgruntled Albanians with successful anti-government protests in Serbia and Bulgaria, planned a weekend rally in Tirana and other cities to press for President Sali Berisha's administration to quit.

In Vlore, a city with a tradition for fierce national sentiment, crowds of up to 30,000 poured through the streets, massing in front of administrative offices and the local headquarters of Berisha's Democratic Party.

"Give us back our money!" the crowd shouted outside the offices, guarded by rows of policemen. "Vlore police, take off your uniforms, join us!" cried the marchers. Demonstrators dispersed before noon and pledged to regroup after nightfall.

Police gave up attempts to disperse protesters earlier this week and allow them to move at will in spontaneous gatherings. No leaders head columns and neither government nor opposition politicians are in evidence.

Two young boys on horseback had led the procession down the city's main palm-lined boulevard. The marchers paused twice to persuade students in a high school and technical college to leave their classrooms and go into the street.

The Vlore protests were sparked by the collapse this week of the Gjallica firm, with about $500 million in deposits. Virtually every family in the region had invested in the firm and protesters vow to gather every day until they get refunds.

"This problem cannot be solved overnight," said Petref Lameborshi, a local Democratic Party member of parliament. "It's like wheat. You plant it in October and reap it in June. You can't reap it in February just because people demand it."
In Tirana, eyewitnesses said investors massed outside the home of Sude, a Gypsy woman who ran a pyramid scheme which failed with 100,000 depositors owed about $60 million.
Riot police arrived in force and dispersed the gathering. Sude is one of several pyramid scheme operators under arrest.

Schemes offering quick, lucrative returns have flourished in post-Communist Albania. Protesters accuse Berisha of failing to warn of the pitfalls and some opposition politicians say the Democratic Party used their proceeds to win re-election last year in polls denounced as unfair by Western observers.
Economists say some $2 billion was invested altogether. Depositors are now receiving partial refunds of deposits from two failed firms but payouts are slow and chaotic.

The Forum for Democracy, a newly-created alliance of nine parties led by the Socialists, appealed in Tirana newspapers for a rally on Saturday in central Skanderbeg Square and in other towns throughout the country of 3.4 million.
"We are calling for mass protests like in other Balkan countries," Socialist Party spokesman Kastriot Islami told Reuters Television.
Berisha has made no public appearances since chairing cross-party talks on Tuesday boycotted by the Forum.
Tirana newspapers said an attempt to discuss the latest protests in parliament on Wednesday was cut short by its chairman Pjeter Arbnori, a staunch Berisha supporter.

Southern Albania was the focal point of protests last month when investors set fire to buildings. Would-be protesters have since been deterred by at least 150 arrests and the threat of 15-year jail terms on public order charges.
